claim: The SIM is a network motif where a single TF regulates the expression of a set of genes, including itself.
source: The SIM is a network motif where a single TF regulates the expression of a set of genes, including itself (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the SIM motif structure, supported by reference to Figure 1A which illustrates this architecture.

claim: In E. coli, the SIM motif is prevalent with the majority of TFs being autoregulated and having multiple targets.
source: In E. coli, this motif is prevalent; the majority of TFs are autoregulated and have multiple targets (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019, which provides evidence for the prevalence of this motif in E. coli.

claim: The purpose of the SIM motif is to coordinate, in both time and magnitude, expression of related genes.
source: Typically, this group of genes have related functions and the purpose of this motif is to coordinate, in both time and magnitude, expression of these related genes (Alon, 2006).
evidence: This functional claim is supported by citation to Alon, 2006, which discusses the coordination function of the SIM motif.

claim: Temporal ordering of gene expression in the SIM motif naturally follows the functional order of genes in the physiological pathway in diverse biological contexts.
source: There are mounting examples, from diverse topics that range from metabolism (Figure 1B, Zaslaver et al., 2004), stress response (Figure 1C, Friedman et al., 2005; Ronen et al., 2002), development (Arnone, 2002; Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Kalir et al., 2001), and cancer (Lorenzin et al., 2016), where temporal ordering of gene expression in the motif naturally follows the functional order of the genes in the physiological pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations across different biological contexts (metabolism, stress response, development, cancer) and reference to figures showing examples.

claim: Temporal ordering in the SIM motif is thought to be set through differential affinity for the TF amongst the various target genes.
source: Mechanistically, it is thought that this ordering is set through differential affinity for the TF amongst the various target genes in the motif (Alon, 2006), although in some experiments temporal ordering was not observed implying a dependence on physiology or another experimental detail that is yet unrecognized (Gerosa et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is supported by citation to Alon, 2006, with additional citations noting exceptions that suggest physiological dependencies.

claim: 62% of TF genes in E. coli are autoregulated, with 42% negatively autoregulated and 20% positively autoregulated.
source: Inset shows different modes of regulation of the TF genes. 62% of the TF genes are autoregulated with 42% negatively autoregulated and 20% positively auotregulated.
evidence: This quantitative claim is presented in the text and shown in the inset of Figure 1D, representing data analysis of E. coli TF regulation patterns.

claim: Increasing the number of decoy sites increases the expression of the auto-repressed TF gene monotonically.
source: We find that increasing the number of decoy sites increases the expression of the auto-repressed TF gene monotonically.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 2A, demonstrating the relationship between decoy sites and TF gene expression.

claim: Despite increased average number of TFs in the cell, the number of unbound TFs decreases as the number of competing binding sites increases.
source: The solid line demonstrates that on average, despite the increased average number of TFs in the cell, the number of unbound TFs decreases as the number of competing binding sites increases (Nevozhay et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B and cited work from Nevozhay et al., 2009.

claim: The expression of the target gene increases as more decoy binding sites are added even though the total number of TFs is also increasing.
source: Just as in the case of the TF gene, we once again see that the expression of the target gene increases as more decoy binding sites are added even though the total number of TFs is also increasing (red points and line).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (blue points) and simulation results (blue lines) shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Even when the regulatory region of the auto-repressed gene and the target gene are identical, the expression (fold-change) is higher for the target gene.
source: Even when the regulatory region of the auto-repressed gene and the target gene are identical, we find that the expression (fold-change or FC) is higher for the target gene, raising the question of how two genes with identical promoters and regulatory binding sites in the same cell can have different regulation levels.
evidence: This observation of regulatory asymmetry is supported by quantitative inspection of data in Figure 2A.

claim: The simple deterministic model predicts a 'symmetric' response for identical regulatory regions.
source: This calculation is applicable for both the TF and the target gene and would predict a 'symmetric' response for identical regulatory regions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the deterministic model equation which does not distinguish between TF and target genes with identical regulatory sequences.

claim: The simple deterministic model performs well for predicting fold-change when the TF is induced or constitutively expressed across a wide range of perturbations.
source: This model performs well for this same promoter in a related system where the TF is induced or constitutively expressed and predicts the fold-change for a wide range of perturbations such as promoter strength, TF-binding site, induction condition and TF competition levels are tuned (data accumulated in Figure 3A, adapted from Phillips et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by accumulated data shown in Figure 3A, adapted from Phillips et al., 2019, demonstrating model performance across various conditions.

claim: For autoregulatory circuits with strong binding sites (O1), neither the target nor the TF gene follow the deterministic solution.
source: However, for the autoregulatory circuits, we find that for strong binding sites (O1) neither the target nor the TF gene follow the deterministic solution (black dashed line).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3C comparing autoregulatory circuit behavior to deterministic predictions.

claim: In autoregulatory circuits with O1 binding sites, the asymmetry occurs with the TF gene being more repressed and the target gene less repressed than expected from the deterministic model.
source: In this case, the asymmetry occurs with the TF gene being more repressed and the target gene less repressed than expected.
evidence: This observation is supported by comparison of simulation data to deterministic predictions in Figure 3C.

claim: For both simulations and experiments of the SIM system, the TF gene is more strongly regulated than the target gene subject to identical regulatory sequences.
source: However, for both simulations and experiments of this system the TF gene is clearly more strongly regulated than the target gene subject to identical regulatory sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by both simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 3D (yellow data points and lines).

claim: When Oid regulates the target gene and O1 regulates the TF gene, the regulation is roughly symmetric despite the target gene having a much stronger binding site.
source: However, when Oid regulates the target gene and O1 regulates the TF gene, the regulation is now roughly symmetric despite the target gene having a much stronger binding site; in this case, the size of the inherent regulatory asymmetry effect is on par with altering the binding site to a stronger operator resulting in symmetric overall regulation of the genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental and simulation data shown in Figure 3D (blue lines and data points).

claim: The asymmetry must originate from differences in states 2 and 3, where either the TF gene or target gene is bound by TF.
source: It should be clear that state 1 and state 4 cannot be the cause of asymmetry; both genes are either fully on (state 1) or fully off (state 4). As such, the asymmetry must originate from differences in states 2 and 3.
evidence: This is a logical inference from analyzing the four possible promoter occupancy states shown in Figure 4A.

claim: State 2 must have an (on average) higher concentration of TF than state 3 because the system is still making TF in state 2, while production of TF is shut off in state 3.
source: Since unbinding rate of a TF is identical for both promoters in our model, the asymmetry must originate from differences in binding of free TF in state 2 and in state 3; specifically state 2 must have an (on average) higher concentration of TF than state 3. This makes sense since the system is still making TF in state 2, while production of TF is shut off in state 3.
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is based on logical inference from the model structure and is validated by simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: State 2 has on average more free TFs than state 3, and as a result, the system spends less time in state 2 than in state 3.
source: Figure 4B validates this interpretation as we can see that state 2 has on average more free TFs than state 3, and as a result, the system spends less time in state 2 than in state 3 in our simulations.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Using the chemical master equation approach, the asymmetry is exactly equal to the difference in time spent in state 3 and state 2, for any condition or parameter choice.
source: Using the chemical master equation (CME) approach, we find that the asymmetry is exactly equal to the difference in time spent in state 3 and state 2, for any condition or parameter choice (Figure 4C and Appendix 9 Equation A9-9: CME for minimal model).
evidence: This theoretical result is derived from the CME formalism as detailed in Appendix 9 and validated by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The general approach of ODEs does not account for differential TF concentration in different states and hence shows no asymmetry.
source: The general approach of ODEs outlined above (Figure 2C) does not account for this differential TF concentration and hence shows no asymmetry.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the simple ODE model based on its mathematical structure.

claim: A modified deterministic model that keeps track of each state and its specific TF concentration can predict asymmetry.
source: Armed with the knowledge that individual states have this systematic TF difference, we can rewrite the basic deterministic model where we instead keep track individually of each state and the specific TF concentration of that state using the same equilibrium mass action kinetic approach (details in Appendix 10: Modified ODEs for the minimal model). Like the stochastic CMEs, the modified ODEs predict that the asymmetry arises from the difference in the TF concentrations in different states and solely depends on the difference in time spent in state 3 (only target gene occupied) and state 2 (only TF gene occupied).
evidence: This theoretical development is detailed in Appendix 10 and represents an inference about how to modify the deterministic model to capture asymmetry.

claim: The modified deterministic model does not quantitatively agree with stochastic modeling results due to not accounting for variability in TF number in each state.
source: Although we find the modified deterministic model can predict asymmetry, it still does not quantitatively agree with the results of stochastic modeling due to the deterministic model not accounting for variability in TF number in each state (see Appendix 10: Modified ODEs for the minimal model).
evidence: This limitation of the modified deterministic model is identified through comparison with stochastic simulations, as detailed in Appendix 10.

claim: The deviation of expression of both TF and target gene from deterministic predictions is more prominent for a strong binding site (Oid or O1) compared to a weaker binding site (O2).
source: This is also evident from Figure 3B,C where we find that the deviation of the expression of both TF and target gene is more prominent for a strong binding site (Oid or O1) compared to a weaker binding site (O2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation data across different binding sites shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Tuning the rates of target gene production and decay has no effect on asymmetry.
source: First, we find that tuning the rates of target gene production and decay has no effect on asymmetry (Appendix 7—figure 1B and Appendix 11—figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in the referenced appendix figures.

claim: The biggest driver of asymmetry among TF production and decay parameters is the protein degradation rate.
source: However, we find that the biggest driver of asymmetry in this set of parameters is the protein degradation rate (Appendix 7—figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation in simulations shown in Appendix 7—figure 1B.

claim: Maximum asymmetry is expected for TF lifetimes between 10 and 100 min, which coincides with typical doubling time of E. coli.
source: Crucially, this maximum coincides with typical doubling time of E. coli (which sets the TF half-life [Marr, 1991; Neidhardt and Curtiss, 1996]) and thus regulatory asymmetry in this motif is most relevant in common physiological conditions.
evidence: This claim connects simulation predictions from Figure 4E with physiological relevance, supported by citations about E. coli doubling times.

claim: For slow degradation, the number of TFs in a cell is high, favoring rapid transition to state 4, thereby reducing the residence times of both state 2 and 3.
source: For slow degradation, the number of TFs in a cell is high, favoring the transition to state 4 very quickly, thereby reducing the residence times of both state 2 and 3.
evidence: This mechanistic explanation for the non-monotonic behavior of asymmetry with degradation rate is based on inference from the model dynamics.

claim: When degradation is fast, the TF number is too low for the cell to be in state 2 or 3; the cell spends most of the time in state 1.
source: On the other extreme, when degradation is fast, the TF number is too low for the cell to be in the state 2 or 3; the cell spends most of the time in state 1.
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is based on inference from the model dynamics at high degradation rates.

claim: In the intermediate regime of degradation, the number of TFs is optimum to maximize the difference between residence times in state 2 and 3, which leads to maximum asymmetry.
source: In the intermediate regime of degradation, the number of TFs is optimum to maximize the difference between residence times in state 2 and 3, which leads to maximum asymmetry.
evidence: This mechanistic explanation synthesizes the behavior at extreme degradation rates to explain the intermediate maximum.

claim: The slowest degradation tag (DAS) introduces strong asymmetry in experiments.
source: Here, we see that the slowest tag (blue points) introduces strong asymmetry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F (blue points).

claim: For the DAS+4 tag, there is a significant decrease in asymmetry compared to the DAS tag, with asymmetry levels similar to the absence of tags.
source: However, for the next fastest tag (green points) we see a significant decrease in asymmetry and the level of regulatory asymmetry is similar to what is seen in the absence of tags (yellow points).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F comparing green and yellow data points.

claim: The fastest degradation tag (LAA) shows no asymmetry at all.
source: Finally, the fastest tag (red points) shows no asymmetry at all.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F (red points).

claim: Controlling the protein degradation rate through synthetic degradation tags agrees with model predictions.
source: Importantly, controlling the protein degradation rate through this synthetic tool agrees with our model predictions, although the actual in vivo protein degradation rates are difficult to estimate from tag sequence alone, the asymmetry follows the expected trends based on the known (and observed) effectiveness of each tag (see schematic inset Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 4F with model predictions, showing qualitative agreement.

claim: According to model predictions, asymmetry should be highest for fast growing cells and decrease (or vanish) for very slow growing cells.
source: According to the model predictions in Figure 4E, the asymmetry should be highest for fast growing cells (roughly 20 min division rate for our growth conditions which is well below the degradation rate for peak asymmetry ∼10 min, Figure 4F) and decrease (or vanish) for very slow growing cells.
evidence: This prediction is based on the heat map shown in Figure 4E relating degradation rate (set by growth rate) to asymmetry.

claim: Faster growing cells show more regulatory asymmetry and slower growing cells show little-to-no regulatory asymmetry.
source: As predicted, faster growing cells show more regulatory asymmetry and slower growing cells show little-to-no regulatory asymmetry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data across different growth conditions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: O2 regulation is symmetric at all studied growth rates.
source: Despite this complication, it is clear that O2 regulation is symmetric at all studied growth rates while Oid regulation is asymmetric for all growth rates with faster growth rates appearing more asymmetric.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B across different growth conditions.

claim: Oid regulation is asymmetric for all growth rates with faster growth rates appearing more asymmetric.
source: Despite this complication, it is clear that O2 regulation is symmetric at all studied growth rates while Oid regulation is asymmetric for all growth rates with faster growth rates appearing more asymmetric.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C across different growth conditions.

claim: The regulatory asymmetry is not due to a small population of outliers, bimodality or any other 'rare' phenotype.
source: Importantly, the regulatory asymmetry is not due to a small population of outliers, bimodality or any other 'rare' phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell histogram data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating that asymmetry is a population-wide phenomenon.

claim: At the highest growth rate and competition level, almost every single cell is expressing target at a higher level than TF.
source: However, as competition levels are increased, the fast-growing conditions shift to higher asymmetry levels; strikingly at the highest growth rate almost every single cell is expressing target at a higher level than TF (bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell histogram data shown in Figure 5D (bottom panel).

claim: There is a fundamental asymmetry in gene regulation that can occur in the SIM regulatory motif that is not related to distinctions in biological processes but rather originates from the way the motif itself is wired.
source: We find that there is a fundamental asymmetry in gene regulation that can occur in the SIM regulatory motif. This asymmetry is not related to distinctions in the biological processes or an unexpected difference in our in vivo experiment, but rather an inherent asymmetry originating from the way the motif itself is wired.
evidence: This is a summary claim synthesizing the findings of the study, supported by the collective experimental and simulation data presented.

claim: Two identical promoters in the same cell with the same average protein concentrations experience distinct regulatory environments in the SIM motif.
source: Although two identical promoters are in the same cell with the same average protein concentrations, they experience distinct regulatory environments.
evidence: This claim summarizes the key finding about differential regulatory environments, supported by the experimental and simulation data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The TF gene has an inherent 'affinity advantage' due to being exposed to systematically higher TF concentrations than its target genes.
source: This is particularly relevant for the SIM motif because the primary function of the motif, organizing and coordinating gene expression patterns, operates on the premise of differential affinities amongst target genes; here we have shown that the TF gene has an inherent 'affinity advantage' due to being exposed to systematically higher TF concentrations than its target genes.
evidence: This interpretive claim is based on the mechanistic understanding developed from the data showing differential TF concentrations in different states.

claim: The TF gene will respond 'earlier' than expected based on the raw affinity of its binding site.
source: This implies that the TF gene will respond 'earlier' than expected based on the raw affinity of its binding site and may necessitate weaker sites on autoregulating TF genes in order to achieve similar timing in expression compared to its targets.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional implications of the asymmetry for temporal ordering in the SIM motif.

claim: Regulatory asymmetry is intrinsic to the negative SIM motif even in the absence of decoys.
source: Regulatory asymmetry is intrinsic to the negative SIM motif even in the absence of decoys, but it can be greatly exacerbated by competing TF-binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing asymmetry at zero decoy sites (Figure 3D) and increasing asymmetry with more decoys.

claim: The magnitude of the asymmetry is enough to compensate for swapping the wild-type proximal O1 LacI binding site on the target gene with the 'ideal' operator Oid.
source: In our system, the magnitude of the asymmetry is enough to compensate for swapping the wild-type proximal O1 LacI binding site on the target gene with the 'ideal' operator Oid.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 3D showing that O1 TF with Oid target produces symmetric regulation.

claim: TF-binding affinity and TF degradation rate are primary drivers of asymmetry in the SIM motif.
source: As such, asymmetry is magnified by anything that enhances this concentration difference. Here, we have identified TF-binding affinity and TF degradation rate (controlled both directly and through modulating growth rate) as primary drivers of asymmetry in this motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic variation of these parameters in simulations (Figure 4E) and experiments (Figures 4F and 5).

claim: This work presents a challenge for the drive to 'read' and predict regulation levels from the promoter DNA alone, as the regulatory motif is responsible for altering the observed regulation and must be considered as well.
source: This work clearly presents a challenge for the drive to 'read' and predict regulation levels from the promoter DNA alone, in this case the regulatory motif is responsible for altering the observed regulation and must be considered as well.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the broader implications of the findings for the field of gene regulation.

claim: Regulatory asymmetry in the SIM motif is a distinct phenomenon that does not operate through an enzymatic process but rather is a fundamental feature of the network.
source: It has previously been demonstrated that features of a transcript can impact its regulation by effects such as targeted degradation, stabilization or posttranslational modification and regulation (Schikora-Tamarit et al., 2018), it is important to point out that regulatory asymmetry in this motif is a distinct phenomenon that does not operate through an enzymatic processes but rather is a fundamental feature of the network.
evidence: This claim distinguishes the mechanism of asymmetry from other known regulatory mechanisms, with citation to related work.

claim: Specific genes can be exposed to systematically different levels of regulatory TFs even in the absence of specific cellular mechanisms such as cytoplasmic compartmentalization, protein localization or DNA accessibility.
source: The broader point that specific genes can be exposed to systematically different levels of regulatory TFs even in the absence of specific cellular mechanisms such as cytoplasmic compartmentalization, protein localization or DNA accessibility is likely more generally relevant.
evidence: This is a generalization of the findings beyond the specific SIM motif studied, based on the mechanistic insights gained.

claim: ArgR is a transcriptional regulator of arginine biosynthesis that auto-regulates itself and genes involved in different steps of arginine biosynthesis.
source: (B) ArgR is a transcriptional regulator of arginine biosynthesis. It auto-regulates itself and genes involved in different steps of arginine biosynthesis with precision in expression starting from the first enzyme of the pathway down to the last.
evidence: This is a description of a biological example of the SIM motif shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the ArgR system, precise ordering of gene expression is thought to originate from a corresponding ordering in TF-binding affinities of the target genes.
source: This precise ordering is thought to originate from a corresponding ordering in TF-binding affinities of the target genes.
evidence: This mechanistic explanation for the ArgR system is based on established understanding in the field.

claim: LexA is the master regulator of SOS pathway and is actively degraded in response to DNA damage.
source: (C) LexA is the master regulator of SOS pathway and is actively degraded in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a description of another biological example of the SIM motif shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LexA auto-represses itself and represses a set of other genes involved in DNA repair.
source: LexA auto-represses itself and represses a set of other genes involved in DNA repair.
evidence: This describes the regulatory architecture of the LexA SIM motif.

claim: In the LexA system, early response genes have low affinity for the repressor while late acting genes have high affinity, enabling temporal ordering of the response.
source: In this case, the early response genes have low affinity for the repressor while the late acting genes have high affinity, enabling temporal ordering of the response.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of temporal ordering in the LexA SIM motif.

claim: The stochastic simulation makes accurate predictions of the asymmetry and its dependence on the parameters of the model that are confirmed through in vivo measurements.
source: The stochastic simulation makes accurate predictions of the asymmetry and its dependence on the parameters of the model that we confirm through in vivo measurements.
evidence: This summary claim is supported by the agreement between simulation predictions and experimental data throughout the Results section.

claim: Regulatory asymmetry is not captured by a simple deterministic model based on mass action equilibrium kinetics.
source: Interestingly, regulatory asymmetry is not captured by a simple deterministic model which is based on translating the stochastic reactions to kinetic rates through mass action equilibrium kinetics (which have been shown to accurately predict target gene expression in other studies [Brewster et al., 2014; Garcia and Phillips, 2011; Garcia et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2014; Razo-Mejia et al., 2018]).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of deterministic model predictions with simulation and experimental data, with citations to studies where the deterministic model worked well.

claim: The simple deterministic model fails to accurately predict expression of either the TF gene or the target gene in the autoregulatory SIM motif.
source: In fact, this deterministic model fails to accurately predict expression of either gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 3C showing deviation of both genes from deterministic predictions.

claim: A revised deterministic model that explicitly allows for different microenvironments in each 'regulatory state' predicts asymmetry.
source: A revised deterministic model, which explicitly allows for different microenvironments in each 'regulatory state', predicts asymmetry, although it still does not recover quantitative agreement with stochastic simulations.
evidence: This claim about the modified deterministic model is based on theoretical development detailed in Appendix 10.

claim: The revised deterministic model still does not recover quantitative agreement with stochastic simulations.
source: A revised deterministic model, which explicitly allows for different microenvironments in each 'regulatory state', predicts asymmetry, although it still does not recover quantitative agreement with stochastic simulations.
evidence: This limitation is noted based on comparison of the modified deterministic model with stochastic results, as discussed in Appendix 10.

claim: In E. coli, roughly 60% of TF genes are autoregulated and almost 70% of those TFs negatively regulate their own expression.
source: As such, in this work, we will focus on a TF that is a negative regulator of its target genes and itself; this is the most common regulation strategy in Escherichia coli where roughly 60% of TF genes are autoregulated and almost 70% of those TFs negatively regulate their own expression (inset Figure 1D, Shen-Orr et al., 2002).
evidence: This statistical claim about E. coli TF regulation is supported by citation to Shen-Orr et al., 2002 and data shown in Figure 1D inset.

claim: Past work with LacI has demonstrated the ability to control with precision the regulatory function, binding affinity and TF copy number through basic sequence level manipulations.
source: Past work with LacI has demonstrated the ability to control with precision the regulatory function, binding affinity and TF copy number through basic sequence level manipulations (Brewster et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2008; Garcia and Phillips, 2011; Jones et al., 2014; Kuhlman et al., 2007; Oehler et al., 1990; Razo-Mejia et al., 2018);
evidence: This claim about the tunability of LacI is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Auto-regulated TF (lacI-mCherry) is expressed from the ybcN locus and the TF-repressed target (yfp) is expressed from the galK locus with identical promoter sequence for both.
source: Auto-regulated TF (lacI-mCherry) is expressed from the ybcN locus and the TF-repressed target (yfp) is expressed from the galK locus with identical promoter sequence for both the TF and the target.
evidence: This describes the genetic construction of the experimental system.

claim: Decoys are introduced on the pZE plasmid.
source: Decoys are introduced on the pZE plasmid.
evidence: This describes how competing binding sites are introduced in the experimental system.

claim: Three different ssrA tags were added to the C-terminus of the LacI-mCherry fusion protein to tune the degradation rate of the TF.
source: In order to tune the degradation rate of the TF, three different ssrA tags were added to the C-terminus of the LacI-mCherry fusion protein. The tags used in this study are wild-type LAA tag (AANDENYALAA), DAS tag (AANDENYADAS) and DAS + 4 tag (AANDENYSENYADAS) (McGinness et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for controlling TF degradation rate, with citation to the source of the tag sequences.

claim: For protein degradation tag experiments with LacI-mCherry fusion protein, HG105 with ΔsspB knockout is used as a parent strain to substantially moderate the protein degradation rate.
source: For protein degradation tag experiments with LacI-mCherry fusion protein, HG105 with ΔsspB knockout is used as a parent strain to substantially moderate the protein degradation rate.
evidence: This describes a modification to the experimental system to control degradation rates.

claim: Deletion of sspB gene did not affect the growth rate in any of the strains tested.
source: It is also noteworthy that deletion of sspB gene did not affect the growth rate in any of the strains tested.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the effect of the sspB deletion.

claim: 0.25% of YFP signals can be seen in the mCherry channel whereas mCherry channel has no crosstalk in the YFP channel.
source: We find that under our microscope 0.25% (γcross=0.0025) of YFP signals can be seen in the mCherry channel whereas mCherry channel has no crosstalk in the YFP channel.
evidence: This is a measurement of fluorescence crosstalk in the microscopy system.

claim: At least 500 individual cells were analyzed per sample.
source: At least 500 individual cells were analyzed per sample and binned according to the mCherry values.
evidence: This describes the sample size for the microscopy analysis.
